4. How to Identify a DP Problem

blocks.text: Dynamic Programming (DP) is a method to solve problems by breaking them into smaller subproblems, solving each one once, and storing the result so you never repeat work.
Think of it as "smart recursion with a memory."
Without DP, some recursive solutions recompute the same thing thousands of times exponential time.
With DP, each subproblem is solved exactly once linear time. The saving is massive.

Note

GPS navigation (shortest path)

Instead of checking all routes again and again, it stores best distances to each city and reuses them to find the shortest path faster.
<hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
Optimal substructure the best answer to the big problem can be built from best answers to smaller ones.
Overlapping subproblems the same smaller problems keep appearing as you recurse, making it worth caching results.
Here's how DP fits into the bigger picture of algorithm types:
We start with a problem and try to break it into smaller subproblems. After breaking it, we analyze the nature of these subproblems.

items: If the subproblems are completely independent and do not repeat, we use Divide & Conquer. In this approach, each part is solved separately and then all results are combined (merged) to get the final answer.

If the subproblems are not independent and the same work repeats again and again, we use Dynamic Programming. Instead of recomputing, we store the results and reuse them whenever needed. This avoids repeated work and improves efficiency.

If the problem allows us to make a direct best choice at every step without worrying about future consequences, we use a Greedy approach. Here, we always pick the locally best option and assume it leads to the global best solution.

blocks.text: Simple Flow:
Break the problem → understand subproblems → choose the right technique → apply the method to get an efficient solution.

Start with a big problem.
Break it into smaller subproblems and define how they relate (recurrence).
For each subproblem:

items: If it is already solved → just take the answer from cache and return immediately
If it is not solved → compute it first, store the result, then return it

blocks.text: Solve each subproblem once, store it, and reuse it whenever needed

content.title: 3. Two Ways In DP (Approaches)

blocks.text: Every DP problem can be solved two ways top-down (memoization) or bottom-up (tabulation).
Let's walk through all 4 approaches using Fibonacci.
1. Naive recursion (the broken way)
Before DP, let's see what goes wrong. fib(5) calls fib(4) and fib(3). But fib(4) also calls fib(3) again. And so on. The same work repeats exponentially.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406029800-81780516.png
Each call to fib(n) makes two more calls: fib(n-1) and fib(n-2). This keeps branching out, so calls grow very fast.
The problem is the same values are recomputed again and againlike fib(3) twice, fib(2) three times.
Because of this, total calls become huge (over a trillion for fib(50)), giving O(2ⁿ) time, which is impractical.
2. Memoization (top-down DP)
Same recursion, but before returning any result, store it in a dictionary. Next time the same fib(n) is called return from cache instantly, no recomputation.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406029800-878914794.png
The first time fib(3) is called, it is not in the cache, so the function computes it by calling fib(2) and fib(1). After computing the result, it stores it in the memo map.
Later, when fib(3) is needed again, instead of recomputing, the function simply looks it up in the map and returns it instantly.
This way, every value from 0 to n is computed only once, and all future calls reuse the stored result.

Time Complexity: O(n) (each value computed once)
Space Complexity: O(n) (for recursion stack + memo storage
3. Tabulation (bottom-up DP)
Forget recursion entirely. Start from the smallest known values and fill a table left to right.
By the time you need fib(n), all smaller values are already sitting in the table.
In this approach, we don’t use recursion at all.
We start from the smallest known values and build the answer step by step. fill every cell left to right no recursion needed.

items:
Then compute next values using previous ones:
dp[2] = dp[1] + dp[0] = 1
dp[3] = dp[2] + dp[1] = 2
dp[4] = dp[3] + dp[2] = 3
dp[5] = dp[4] + dp[3] = 5
dp[6] = dp[5] + dp[4] = 8

blocks.text: Each value depends on already computed values, so everything is ready when needed.
Start small → build up → store in table → no repeated work

Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
4. Space optimisation
Look at the tabulation code to compute dp[i] you only ever need the two previous values.
You don't need the whole array. Just keep two variables and roll them forward.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406115431-347366731.png
What’s happening:

We don’t use a full DP array anymore.
Instead of storing all values, we keep only two variables:
At each step:

So the window keeps moving forward like:
(a, b) → (b, next)
We only keep track of the last two values, because that’s all we need.
This removes the need for the whole DP table.

Time Complexity: O(n)
Space Complexity: O(1) (constant space, no array)

content.title: 4. How to Identify a DP Problem

blocks.text: Ask these 3 questions:

• Can I break the problem into smaller subproblems?
  • Do the same subproblems repeat?
  • Can I store and reuse answers?
